title: C and C++: how safe can you get without a rewrite?
short: Ship every build with the OpenSSF hardening flags and a bounds-checked standard library (0.3% overhead at Google), fuzz parsers under ASan and write new components in a memory-safe language.
answer: Before your next release, build with the OpenSSF hardening flags and a bounds-checked standard library, and run your tests and fuzzers under AddressSanitizer and UBSan in CI. Write new components in a memory-safe language, and judge every other change by whether it checks the size, owner and lifetime of memory that outside data reaches.
audience: Developers and tech leads maintaining production C and C++, and the security people who review it

blocks.title: If you only do five things
blocks.intro: Seven of the 2025 CWE Top 25 are buffer overflows, out-of-bounds access, use after free or NULL dereference[^cwe25]. Memory-safety bugs fell from 76% of Android's vulnerabilities in 2019 to under 20% in 2025 as new code moved to memory-safe languages[^gsource][^android].

items.title: Build every release with the OpenSSF hardening flags.
items.text: For GCC and Clang these include `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`, `-fstack-protector-strong`, `-fstack-clash-protection`, `-Wl,-z,relro`, `-Wl,-z,now`, `-fPIE -pie` and `-ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero`[^openssf]; GCC's `-fhardened` sets most at once[^gccinst]. On MSVC, add `/guard:cf` and `/CETCOMPAT`[^mscfg][^mscet].

items.title: Bounds-check the standard library in production.
items.text: Define `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS`, set libc++ to `_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_FAST`[^openssf][^libcxx] or define `_MSVC_STL_HARDENING=1`[^msstl]. At Google it cost 0.3% on average, found over 1,000 bugs and cut segfaults by 30%[^gretro].

items.title: Run every test under ASan and UBSan.
items.text: `-fsanitize=address` catches out-of-bounds access and use after free at about half speed[^asan], `-fsanitize=undefined` integer overflow and other undefined behavior[^ubsan]. Leave `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` out of these builds[^openssf].

items.title: Fuzz every parser of outside data.
items.text: Give each file format, protocol and decoder a libFuzzer target, and run it on every pull request with ClusterFuzzLite under ASan, MSan and UBSan[^cflite].

items.title: Write new components in a memory-safe language.
items.text: Five-year-old code has 3.4 to 7.4 times lower vulnerability density than new code[^gsource]. CISA and the FBI asked makers of C and C++ products to publish a memory-safety roadmap by the end of 2025[^cisabad]. See the Rust sheet.

blocks.title: Review a C or C++ pull request

items.title: Does a length, count or offset come from the input?
items.text: Check it against the bytes left and the destination's size before any copy, index or allocation.

items.title: Can a size calculation wrap?
items.text: Look for `*` and `+` on sizes, `int` lengths and signed-to-unsigned casts. Ask for `__builtin_mul_overflow`[^gccovf].

items.title: Who owns each pointer, and can anything outlive it?
items.text: Check raw `new`, `delete` and `free`, stored `string_view` and `span` members, and callbacks that capture `this` or `&`.

items.title: Is every error code and union tag checked?
items.text: Ask for `[[nodiscard]]` on functions that return errors and a tag check before each union read.

items.title: Does it switch off a check?
items.text: Warning pragmas, `no_sanitize`, `_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_NONE`, `[[indeterminate]]` and `/GS-` need a second reviewer.

blocks.title: C and C++ traps and what to use instead
items: **`memcpy(buf, p, len)` with `len` from the input.** OpenSSL copied an AEAD IV from ASN.1 parameters into a fixed-size stack buffer without checking that it fit, before any authentication (CVE-2025-15467, high)[^openssl]. Check each length against the destination and the bytes left; `_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` catches such copies only when it knows the buffer's size[^openssf].

**`n * size` and `len + 1` in size calculations.** Unsigned arithmetic wraps silently, and signed overflow is undefined, so the compiler may delete your overflow check[^openssf]. Integer overflows in Ruby's C regex engine let crafted patterns run code on GitLab servers; CISA lists CVE-2026-97229 as exploited[^ruby][^kev]. Compute sizes with `__builtin_mul_overflow` and `__builtin_add_overflow`[^gccovf].

**Error codes that let a decoder keep going.** Brotli's decoder reported an invalid block switch as a need for more input and kept appending to an eight-byte buffer (CVE-2026-111497, exploited)[^nodejs][^kev]. Treat each format error as final, check the bound on every append, and mark functions that return errors `[[nodiscard]]`.

**Ownership and lifetimes an API leaves unclear.** OpenSSL's `PKCS7_verify()` freed a BIO its caller still owned, so the caller's own `BIO_free()` became a use after free (CVE-2026-45447, high)[^openssl]. In C++, own with `std::unique_ptr` and don't keep a `std::string_view` or `std::span` past its owner; Clang 23's `-Wlifetime-safety` catches some cases[^clang23]. In C, document who frees each argument.

**Reading a union member or downcast object without checking its type.** OpenSSL read an `ASN1_TYPE` union member without validating the type (CVE-2026-22796)[^openssl], and CISA lists type confusion in Chrome's V8 and in Windows as exploited this year[^kev]. Check the tag before each read; in C++ use `std::variant` and `std::get_if`.

**`printf(msg)` and your own logging wrappers.** OpenSSL passed a peer's distinguished name as the format string to `ERR_raise_data()`, so a name like `CN=%s%n` crashed CMP clients (CVE-2026-63073)[^openssl]. Pass data through `"%s"`, build with `-Werror=format-security`[^openssf] and mark wrappers `format(printf, m, n)` so their callers get checked[^gccattr].

blocks.title: Tools that catch it
items: **Sanitizers.** ASan (about 2x slower), UBSan, MSan for uninitialized reads (needs every library instrumented, even libc) and TSan for data races (5x to 15x)[^asan][^msan][^tsan]. ASan and TSan can't be combined[^openssf]. MSVC has `/fsanitize=address`[^msasan].
**Fuzzers.** libFuzzer gets bug fixes only, as its authors moved to Centipede[^libfuzzer]; ClusterFuzzLite still runs it on pull requests and in batch jobs[^cflite].

**Warnings.** `-Wall`, `-Wextra`, `-Wformat=2`, `-Wconversion`[^openssf] and, in C++, Clang's `-Wunsafe-buffer-usage`, which flags buffer access through raw pointers so you can move it to `std::span`[^safebuf]. On MSVC, `/sdl` turns uninitialized-variable warnings into errors[^mssdl].

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **GCC 16 (30 April) zero-initializes locals under `-std=c++26`,** implements C++26 contracts and erroneous behavior, and defaults to `-std=gnu++20`[^gcc16][^gccopt].
**Clang 23 (26 August) added `-Wlifetime-safety`,** an analysis that detects use after free within a function. Add it to your CI flags[^clang23].

**OpenSSL published 63 CVEs in 2026, against 6 in 2025;** all three High ones are memory-safety bugs[^openssl]. OpenSSL 3.0 reached end of life on 7 September; move to 3.5, supported until April 2030[^openssleol].
**CISA added an exploited Brotli decoder overflow on 27 October.** Update every copy, including vendored ones such as Node.js bundles, to 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1[^cvebrotli][^kev][^nodejs].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **Waiting for C++26.** Its library hardening standardizes checks libc++, libstdc++ and MSVC already ship[^p3471], and `-ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero` initializes locals today[^openssf].
**Rewriting stable code all at once.** Vulnerabilities decay as code ages[^gsource]. Harden old code; rewrite the parsers and network code that take outside data.
**Valgrind in CI.** Sanitizers do similar work at a 2x to 4x slowdown, against 20x to 50x[^openssf]. Keep it for binaries you can't rebuild.

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Checks only debug builds get.** GCC 15's libstdc++ enables its assertions by default only in unoptimized builds[^gcc15], and `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` needs `-O1` or higher[^openssf]. Set both in release builds.

**Shipping sanitizer runtimes.** Their environment-variable options can let attackers clobber root-owned files through setuid binaries. Only UBSan's minimal runtime or trap mode belongs in production[^openssf][^ubsan].

blocks.title: What this looks like for your code

columns.title: New project
items: Ask first whether it can be Rust or another memory-safe language.
If it must be C++, use `std::span` and `std::unique_ptr`, and turn on `-Wunsafe-buffer-usage`[^safebuf].
Start with the OpenSSF flags, a hardened library, sanitizer jobs and a fuzz target per parser.

columns.title: Existing codebase
items: Roll out hardening as Google did: tests first, then pre-production, then production over months[^gretro].
Replace `[0]` and `[1]` trailing arrays with `[]`, then add `-fstrict-flex-arrays=3`[^openssf].
Fuzz network-facing and crypto code first[^cisabad], and publish a date after which new code is memory-safe[^cisaroad].

columns.title: High-assurance or regulated
items: Follow Chromium's Rule of 2: of untrusted input, an unsafe language and high privilege, pick at most two[^ruleof2].
Use libc++ extensive mode where benchmarks allow[^libcxx], and MSan with every library instrumented[^msan].
On Arm cores with MTE, test with memory tagging: GCC 16 adds `-fsanitize=memtag` for the stack[^gcc16].

changes.text: First draft, based on the OpenSSF compiler hardening guide, GCC, Clang, libc++ and MSVC docs, WG21 papers, Google's memory-safety data, CISA and FBI guidance, OpenSSL advisories and the 2025 CWE Top 25.
